builder_plan.scenario: A self-hosted assistant is too expensive because its model uses most of the GPU memory.
builder_plan.change: Try the paper's supported lower-precision weights on a copy of your serving setup.
builder_plan.baseline: The same model at its original precision, on the same GPU.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Peak memory, task pass rate, latency, and total serving cost at the same context and load.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Cruella: A Unified Microscaling and Floating-Point Dot-Product Unit for LLM Inference on FPGAs
summary: Cruella replaces separate MXFP4 and BF16 dot-product units on an FPGA with a single unified unit that executes both product types on one DSP array via per-group pre-alignment and pre-adder packing of two MXFP4xBF16 products into one multiplier. The cost is FPGA-specific hardware design effort, a perplexity change of up to 0.7%, and the continued need to keep attention and KV-cache computation in BF16, which otherwise idles a dedicated MXFP4 unit for 56%-77% of datapath time. It can fail for this reader because the gains are measured only on an Alveo U55C, an A40 GPU still decodes faster in absolute terms, and MXFP4 checkpoint support on commodity GPUs depends on vendor kernel availability rather than anything this paper provides.
rationale: The technique is implemented as a custom FPGA bitstream on specific datacenter hardware (Alveo U55C, DSP48E2), which the reader does not possess, and the paper itself shows an NVIDIA A40 GPU decodes faster, so it offers no actionable path on the reader's 24 GB GPU or API-based infrastructure.

claims.statement: Cruella replaces separate MXFP4 and BF16 dot-product units on an FPGA with a single unified unit that executes both product types on one DSP array via per-group pre-alignment and pre-adder packing of two MXFP4xBF16 products into one multiplier. The cost is FPGA-specific hardware design effort, a perplexity change of up to 0.7%, and the continued need to keep attention and KV-cache computation in BF16, which otherwise idles a dedicated MXFP4 unit for 56%-77% of datapath time. It can fail for this reader because the gains are measured only on an Alveo U55C, an A40 GPU still decodes faster in absolute terms, and MXFP4 checkpoint support on commodity GPUs depends on vendor kernel availability rather than anything this paper provides.

On an Alveo U55C FPGA, MXFP4 weights speed up decoding by 1.15x-1.87x over BF16 weights; an NVIDIA A40 decodes faster but consumes 0.92x-2.01x the board's energy per token. The unified dot-product unit also uses 23% fewer DSP slices and 36% fewer LUTs than separate MXFP4 and BF16 units, with perplexity change of at most 0.7%.
